frameworks.name: Full-Script Pitch Standardization
frameworks.definition: A training framework where every word and visual of a pitch is pre-scripted on slides (one phrase per slide), reducing speaker training time to delivery mechanics only (pace, volume, gesture).

claims.text: Speaker training time is dominated by pitch instability, not by speaking skill. When the pitch is fully standardized into a word-for-word script paired with visuals on slides, training shrinks from months to weeks because the focus becomes purely delivery mechanics: how fast to speak, volume, tone shifts, and hand movements.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Standardization removes variability in pitch content, leaving only delivery as the training variable; this dramatically lowers cognitive load on new speakers.
bounded_by: Does not apply to one-on-one consultative selling where customization per client is required
Does not apply to low-stakes commoditized pitches where speaker quality doesn't drive material conversion differences

claims.text: A fully scripted pitch should be one sentence or phrase maximum per slide, advancing one slide every 6-10 seconds. This keeps attention high through constant visual change and anchors every spoken word to a corresponding visual, maximizing comprehension and enforcing script compliance.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
bounded_by: Does not account for audience comprehension variation or cultural pace differences

claims.text: Alex Hormozi's Money Models pitch used 1,700 slides for a 90-minute presentation, where every word was scripted and paired with a visual. This approach generated $70 million in revenue in one company (transaction size unspecified, time period unspecified).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Adam's business training company runs 12-15 free in-person demonstration events monthly, each drawing approximately 100 business owners. A £1,000 offer at each event converts about 250 new clients per month into a three-day boot camp, generating $14.8 million in annual revenue with target scale to $25 million.
claims.speaker: Adam

claims.text: Boot camp participants face tiered offers ranging from $5,000 (startup track) to $30,000 (advanced track) after a three-day in-person training. Average revenue per attendee is $5,000, indicating a consistent conversion profile across tiers.
claims.speaker: Adam

numbers.axis: boot camp pricing and revenue capture

claims.text: In-person business training and pitch models are resistant to digital-only transition because the value and differentiation are anchored to in-person experience. Attempting to move online significantly erodes the core unit economics of the business model.
claims.speaker: Adam
claims.mechanism: In-person delivery creates trust, relationship, and experiential value that digital environments cannot replicate in business training contexts; online delivery requires different acquisition costs and messaging.
bounded_by: Does not apply to purely information-based products where context and relationship are less critical
Does not account for hybrid or virtual event innovations

claims.text: Speaker training for in-person pitches can be accelerated from months to a week via asynchronous pre-recording: speakers record themselves delivering the standardized pitch 25-50 times from home (90 minutes per take with breaks), submit the best recording, receive feedback at 2x playback speed, and only perform live once pitch quality is validated.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Decoupling feedback from live delivery reduces founder/trainer time and risk of speaker mistakes during high-stakes events. Repetition + self-recording eliminates performer anxiety and enables mastery before live performance.
bounded_by: Requires speaker discipline and self-motivation for unsupervised practice
Does not account for speakers who need real-time feedback or live coaching

claims.text: If the pitch script and delivery are word-perfect, close rates are predictable and high; speaker swaps do not materially change conversion because pitch quality, not speaker personality, drives closes. This has been validated across multiple speaker rotations.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: A pitch that works is replicated by any speaker who delivers it accurately because close mechanisms depend on argument structure and proof, not on speaker charisma or personality.
bounded_by: Does not apply to personal brand sales where founder credibility is the primary value driver
Does not apply to low-structure conversational sales where adaptability is required

claims.text: Adam's business currently has a 50% gross margin business model. By standardizing the speaker pitch and training system, the company can scale from $7 million in profit to $14 million in profit (a 100% profit increase) with only one operational move (pitch standardization and speaker training), without changing pricing, customer base, or the fundamental business model.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: The bottleneck is not economics or market demand, but operational capacity to train new speakers. Removing this constraint via standardization enables all existing margins to scale without reinvention.

numbers.axis: profit scaling from single operational fix

claims.text: The primary constraint blocking scale from $14.8M to $25M revenue is the acquisition method bottleneck: the ability to train new in-person pitchers to match the quality of existing speakers. Geography and speaker availability are secondary constraints. Fixing the pitch standardization removes the binding constraint.
claims.speaker: Adam
claims.mechanism: Speaker training time has been the focus of Adam's year because new speaker ramping directly gates the number of events that can be run and therefore customer acquisition volume.

examples.text: At Money Models (unspecified time period), Alex Hormozi used a 1,700-slide, fully scripted pitch where every word was paired with a visual. This pitch-driven model contributed to generating $70 million in revenue in one of his companies. The extreme slide density was matched by precise timing: advancing one slide roughly every 6-10 seconds kept audience attention constant. By moving all script variation control to the slides, he could swap speakers without materially changing close rates.

Adam's business training company demonstrates the event-to-training pipeline at scale: 12-15 free demonstration events per month attract approximately 100 business owners each (~1,200 attendees per month). A simple £1,000 offer converts roughly 250 of those into boot camp customers, which represents approximately a 21% conversion on initial offer. These boot camp participants then face tiered upsells from $5,000 to $30,000, generating $5,000 average revenue per participant. This produces $14.8 million in annual revenue with 50% gross margins, yielding roughly $7 million in profit.

Adam had trained 6-8 in-person pitchers over time, but the ramp-to-proficiency was slow and inconsistent. New pitchers required extended training to deliver the complex business training message effectively. By implementing a 1,700-slide, fully scripted pitch deck (adopted from Hormozi's model), the training focus shifted from teaching pitch strategy to teaching delivery mechanics only: pace, volume, tone, and hand movements. Speakers could then self-record themselves delivering the pitch 25-50 times from home before ever pitching live to an audience, reducing live-event risk and shortening trainer feedback cycles from months to a week.

practices.text: Transcript the best in-person pitches your company has ever delivered, consolidate them into a master transcript using AI, and convert that into a fully scripted slide deck (one phrase per slide) before training new speakers.

Require new speakers to self-record their pitch delivery 25-50 times from home in 90-minute sessions with breaks between. Have them submit the best recording, provide feedback asynchronously at 2x playback speed, and only deploy them live once quality is validated.

Focus scaling efforts on the binding constraint, not on adding new channels or business lines. If the constraint is speaker training, fix speaker training first before attempting to move online or add adjacent offerings.

In in-person event-based businesses, maintain and expand the in-person event model rather than transitioning to digital-only, because the core value and differentiation are anchored to the physical experience.
